name: D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal
principle: Mandatory safeguards for every arrest and detention.
summary: The Supreme Court laid down binding requirements for arrest and detention to prevent custodial violence: police must carry visible identification, prepare an arrest memo attested by a witness and countersigned by the arrestee, inform a relative or friend, tell the arrestee of this right, conduct medical examination, and allow the arrestee to meet a lawyer during interrogation. Many of these were later written into the criminal procedure code.

name: Lalita Kumari v. Government of Uttar Pradesh
principle: Registration of an FIR is mandatory when information discloses a cognizable offence.
summary: A Constitution Bench held that police must register an FIR if the information discloses a cognizable offence, and no preliminary enquiry is permitted in such a case. A limited preliminary enquiry is allowed only in specified categories such as matrimonial, commercial and medical negligence disputes, and must be completed within a short time. Action must be taken against officers who fail to register an FIR.

name: Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar
principle: No automatic arrest for offences punishable up to seven years.
summary: The Court held that police must not arrest automatically in cases punishable with imprisonment up to seven years, including cruelty cases under Section 498A IPC. Officers must satisfy themselves of the necessity of arrest using a checklist, and Magistrates must not authorise detention mechanically. Failure invites departmental action and contempt.

name: Sakiri Vasu v. State of Uttar Pradesh
principle: If police do not register an FIR, approach the SP and then the Magistrate.
summary: The Court explained that a person whose FIR is not registered should first approach the Superintendent of Police and then the Magistrate, who has wide powers to order registration and to monitor a proper investigation, rather than directly approaching the High Court.

name: Youth Bar Association of India v. Union of India
principle: FIRs must be uploaded online within 24 hours, except sensitive cases.
summary: The Court directed that copies of FIRs be uploaded on police websites within 24 hours of registration so the accused and others can access them, except in sensitive cases such as sexual offences, insurgency and offences against children.

name: Paramvir Singh Saini v. Baljit Singh
principle: CCTV cameras must be installed in all police stations and investigating agencies.
summary: To check custodial violence, the Court directed installation of CCTV cameras with night vision and audio covering entry and exit points, lock-ups, corridors and interrogation rooms of every police station, with footage preserved, and allowed victims of custodial violence to seek the footage.

name: Nilabati Behera v. State of Orissa
principle: The State must pay compensation for custodial death.
summary: The Court held that compensation can be awarded under Article 32 or 226 for violation of the right to life by the State, such as a death in police custody, as a public law remedy separate from any civil suit or criminal prosecution.

name: Prakash Singh v. Union of India
principle: Police reforms including Police Complaints Authorities.
summary: The Court directed police reforms, including the creation of State and District Police Complaints Authorities to inquire into serious misconduct by police officers, separation of investigation from law and order, and fixed tenure for key officers.

name: Satender Kumar Antil v. Central Bureau of Investigation
principle: Bail is the rule and jail the exception; guidelines on bail.
summary: The Court issued comprehensive bail guidelines, categorising offences and holding that where an accused was not arrested during investigation and cooperated, they should ordinarily not be taken into custody when the chargesheet is filed. It stressed compliance with the Arnesh Kumar directions and timely disposal of bail applications.

name: Sushila Aggarwal v. State (NCT of Delhi)
principle: Anticipatory bail need not be limited to a fixed period.
summary: A Constitution Bench held that anticipatory bail need not invariably be limited in time and can continue until the end of trial, though courts may impose conditions depending on the facts.

name: Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan
principle: Sexual harassment at the workplace violates fundamental rights; employers must prevent it.
summary: In the absence of legislation, the Court framed binding guidelines requiring employers to prevent sexual harassment and set up complaints committees headed by a woman, holding that such harassment violates Articles 14, 15, 19 and 21. These guidelines formed the basis of the POSH Act, 2013.

name: Aureliano Fernandes v. State of Goa
principle: Authorities must ensure Internal Committees are properly constituted and functional.
summary: Noting serious gaps in implementation of the POSH Act, the Court directed governments, public authorities and organisations to verify that Internal Committees, Local Committees and Internal Complaints Committees are constituted and their details published, and that members are trained in the procedure.

name: Laxmi v. Union of India
principle: Regulation of acid sale and compensation and free treatment for acid attack survivors.
summary: The Court directed regulation of over-the-counter sale of acid, minimum compensation for acid attack victims from the State, and free medical treatment including reconstructive surgery in private and public hospitals.

name: Nipun Saxena v. Union of India
principle: The identity of victims of rape and of child sexual abuse must never be disclosed.
summary: The Court held that no person may print or publish the name of a victim of rape or child sexual abuse, or any fact from which her identity could be known, including in social media. Police must keep such records in sealed covers.

name: Aparna Bhat v. State of Madhya Pradesh
principle: Courts must not trivialise sexual offences through bail conditions or stereotypes.
summary: The Court set aside a bail condition requiring the accused to have a rakhi tied by the complainant, holding that bail conditions must not mandate contact between the accused and the victim and that judges must avoid gender stereotypes in orders and observations.

name: Independent Thought v. Union of India
principle: Sexual intercourse with a wife below 18 years is rape.
summary: The Court read down the marital rape exception in the IPC so that sexual intercourse by a man with his wife who is below 18 years of age is rape, harmonising the law with POCSO.

name: Attorney General for India v. Satish
principle: Skin-to-skin contact is not required for sexual assault under POCSO.
summary: The Court overturned a High Court ruling and held that the most important ingredient of sexual assault under Section 7 POCSO is sexual intent, not skin-to-skin contact; touching a child's private parts over clothes with sexual intent is sexual assault.

name: Hiral P. Harsora v. Kusum Narottamdas Harsora
principle: Domestic violence complaints can be filed against women and minors too.
summary: The Court struck down the words 'adult male' from the definition of respondent in the Domestic Violence Act, so that a complaint can be filed against female relatives such as a mother-in-law or sister-in-law, and against any person in the domestic relationship.

name: Satish Chander Ahuja v. Sneha Ahuja
principle: A wife's right to reside extends to the in-laws' house where she lived.
summary: A three-judge Bench held that a shared household includes a house belonging to the husband's relatives where the woman lived in a domestic relationship, so she may claim a right of residence there even if her husband has no share in it.

name: Rajnesh v. Neha
principle: Uniform guidelines on maintenance, including mandatory affidavits of disclosure.
summary: The Court laid down guidelines for maintenance under all laws: both parties must file affidavits disclosing assets and liabilities, maintenance is payable from the date of application, overlapping orders must be adjusted, and criteria for fixing the amount were set out.

name: Mohd. Ahmed Khan v. Shah Bano Begum
principle: Divorced Muslim women can claim maintenance under the criminal procedure code.
summary: A Constitution Bench held that the provision for maintenance of wives in the criminal procedure code applies to all persons regardless of religion, including a divorced Muslim woman unable to maintain herself.

name: Danial Latifi v. Union of India
principle: A Muslim husband must make a reasonable and fair provision for the divorced wife's future.
summary: The Court upheld the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act, 1986 by interpreting it to require a reasonable and fair provision for the divorced wife's entire future, to be made within the iddat period.

name: Shayara Bano v. Union of India
principle: Instant triple talaq is unconstitutional.
summary: A Constitution Bench set aside the practice of talaq-e-biddat (instant triple talaq) as manifestly arbitrary and unconstitutional. Parliament later enacted the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Marriage) Act, 2019.

name: Amardeep Singh v. Harveen Kaur
principle: The six-month waiting period for mutual consent divorce can be waived.
summary: The Court held that the six-month cooling-off period under Section 13B(2) of the Hindu Marriage Act is directory, not mandatory, and may be waived where there is no chance of reconciliation and the parties have settled all issues.

name: Vineeta Sharma v. Rakesh Sharma
principle: Daughters have equal coparcenary rights by birth, whether or not the father was alive in 2005.
summary: A three-judge Bench held that a daughter's right as a coparcener under the amended Section 6 of the Hindu Succession Act arises by birth, and does not depend on her father being alive on 9 September 2005.

name: Shakti Vahini v. Union of India
principle: Adults have the right to marry a person of their choice; honour crimes must be prevented.
summary: The Court held that the choice of two consenting adults to marry is protected by Articles 19 and 21, that interference by khap panchayats or families is illegal, and laid down preventive, remedial and punitive measures against honour crimes.

name: Joseph Shine v. Union of India
principle: Adultery is no longer a crime.
summary: A Constitution Bench struck down Section 497 IPC (adultery) as violating Articles 14, 15 and 21, holding that it treated women as the property of their husbands. Adultery may still be a ground for divorce.

name: Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India
principle: Consensual same-sex relations between adults are not a crime.
summary: A Constitution Bench read down Section 377 IPC to decriminalise consensual sexual conduct between adults, holding that sexual orientation is protected by the rights to equality, expression, dignity and privacy.

name: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India
principle: Privacy is a fundamental right.
summary: A nine-judge Bench unanimously held that the right to privacy is a fundamental right protected under Article 21 and Part III of the Constitution, including informational privacy and bodily autonomy, subject to tests of legality, necessity and proportionality.

name: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India
principle: Any procedure depriving personal liberty must be just, fair and reasonable.
summary: The Court held that the procedure established by law under Article 21 must be fair, just and reasonable, not arbitrary, and that Articles 14, 19 and 21 are interlinked. This greatly expanded the scope of the right to life and liberty.

name: Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation
principle: The right to livelihood is part of the right to life.
summary: The Court held that the right to life under Article 21 includes the right to livelihood, and that pavement dwellers could not be evicted without notice and a fair hearing.

name: Hussainara Khatoon v. Home Secretary, State of Bihar
principle: Speedy trial and free legal aid are part of Article 21.
summary: Dealing with thousands of undertrials detained for periods longer than their possible sentences, the Court held that speedy trial is a fundamental right and that the State must provide free legal services to accused persons who cannot afford a lawyer.

name: Shreya Singhal v. Union of India
principle: Section 66A of the IT Act is unconstitutional.
summary: The Court struck down Section 66A of the Information Technology Act, which criminalised 'offensive' online messages, as vague and violating free speech. It also read down intermediary liability so platforms must remove content upon a court order or government notification.

name: Indian Medical Association v. V.P. Shantha
principle: Medical services are covered by consumer protection law.
summary: The Court held that services rendered by medical practitioners and hospitals for a fee fall within the definition of service under consumer protection law, so patients can file consumer complaints for medical negligence. Services rendered entirely free of charge are excluded.

name: Jacob Mathew v. State of Punjab
principle: Criminal liability for medical negligence requires gross negligence.
summary: The Court held that a doctor can be criminally prosecuted for negligence only where the negligence is gross, and that a private complaint against a doctor should be supported by a credible medical opinion. Civil and consumer remedies apply to ordinary negligence.

name: Lucknow Development Authority v. M.K. Gupta
principle: Housing construction is a service, and compensation can include harassment.
summary: The Court held that construction of houses by a development authority is a service under consumer law, and that consumer fora can award compensation for harassment and mental agony caused by deficient service, recoverable from the officers responsible.

name: Pioneer Urban Land and Infrastructure Ltd. v. Govindan Raghavan
principle: One-sided builder agreements are unfair trade practices; homebuyers can seek refund for delay.
summary: The Court held that one-sided clauses in builder-buyer agreements are unfair trade practices and not binding, and that a homebuyer cannot be made to wait indefinitely for possession and is entitled to a refund with compensation for inordinate delay.

name: Meters and Instruments Pvt. Ltd. v. Kanchan Mehta
principle: Cheque bounce cases are primarily compensatory and can be closed on payment.
summary: The Court held that the offence under Section 138 NI Act is primarily a civil wrong with a compensatory purpose, that courts may close proceedings if the accused pays the cheque amount with interest and costs, and encouraged summary trials and settlement.

name: Rame Gowda v. M. Varadappa Naidu
principle: A person in settled possession cannot be evicted except by due process of law.
summary: The Court held that even the true owner cannot forcibly dispossess a person in settled possession of property, and must take recourse to law. The person in settled possession may defend their possession against forcible dispossession.

name: Savelife Foundation v. Union of India
principle: Good Samaritans helping accident victims must be protected.
summary: The Court gave force of law to guidelines protecting Good Samaritans who help road accident victims: they cannot be detained, need not disclose identity, and hospitals cannot demand payment from them. These were later codified in Section 134A of the Motor Vehicles Act.

name: Pt. Parmanand Katara v. Union of India
principle: Every doctor must give immediate medical aid to an injured person; legal formalities cannot delay it.
summary: The Court held that every doctor, in a government or private hospital, has a professional obligation to give immediate medical aid to preserve life, without waiting for police formalities in medico-legal cases.

name: Sarla Verma v. Delhi Transport Corporation
principle: Standard method for computing compensation for death in accidents.
summary: The Court laid down a standardised method for computing compensation in motor accident death claims, including the multiplier based on the deceased's age and deductions for personal expenses based on the number of dependants.

name: National Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Pranay Sethi
principle: Future prospects must be added in computing accident compensation.
summary: A Constitution Bench held that future prospects must be added to the income of the deceased (including self-employed persons) when computing compensation, and fixed standard amounts for loss of estate, consortium and funeral expenses.

name: State of Punjab v. Jagjit Singh
principle: Equal pay for equal work applies to temporary employees.
summary: The Court held that temporary, daily-wage and contractual employees performing the same duties as regular employees are entitled to the minimum of the regular pay scale under the principle of equal pay for equal work.

name: People's Union for Democratic Rights v. Union of India
principle: Paying less than the minimum wage is forced labour.
summary: In a case about workers on Asian Games construction sites, the Court held that paying less than the minimum wage amounts to forced labour prohibited by Article 23, and that labour laws must be enforced against contractors and principal employers.

name: Bandhua Mukti Morcha v. Union of India
principle: The State must identify, release and rehabilitate bonded labourers.
summary: The Court held that bonded labour violates fundamental rights and directed the State to identify, release and rehabilitate bonded labourers working in stone quarries, treating a letter petition as a public interest litigation.

name: CBSE v. Aditya Bandopadhyay
principle: Students can access their evaluated answer sheets under RTI.
summary: The Court held that an evaluated answer book is information under the RTI Act and examinees are entitled to inspect or obtain copies of it, subject to exemptions.

name: Central Public Information Officer, Supreme Court of India v. Subhash Chandra Agarwal
principle: The office of the Chief Justice of India is a public authority under RTI.
summary: A Constitution Bench held that the office of the Chief Justice of India is a public authority under the RTI Act, balancing transparency against privacy and judicial independence on a case-by-case basis.

name: Prathvi Raj Chauhan v. Union of India
principle: The 2018 amendment barring anticipatory bail under the SC/ST Act is valid.
summary: The Court upheld Section 18A of the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, which removed the requirement of a preliminary enquiry before registering an FIR and of approval before arrest, while noting that courts may still quash proceedings where no prima facie case exists.
